library(manimR)
manim_config(verbosity = "WARNING", progress_bar = FALSE)
# The website shows every scene as a video; installed vignettes and
# R CMD check show the last frame of each scene instead.
in_pkgdown <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(format = if (in_pkgdown) "auto" else "png", quality = "l")

An animation changes one or more mobjects over time. This vignette starts
with the two ways to make animations (`self$play()` with an animation
object, and the `$animate` builder), then walks through every family of
animations that manimR provides, and ends with the tools for building your
own: composition, speed changes, rate functions, path functions, class
defaults, overrides and custom R6 animation classes.

Each example is a short scene. On the package website the scenes play as
videos; in the installed vignette you see the last frame of each one.

## Playing animations

A scene is an R6 class that inherits from `Scene` and defines
`construct()`. Inside `construct()`, `self$play()` runs one or more
animations at the same time and `self$wait()` holds the current frame.
`self$add()` and `self$remove()` change what is on screen instantly,
without an animation.

```{manim play-basics}
PlayBasics <- R6::R6Class("PlayBasics", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    square <- Square(color = BLUE)$shift(LEFT * 3)
    circle <- Circle(color = RED)$shift(RIGHT * 3)
    note <- Text("added without animation", font_size = 28)$to_edge(UP)
    self$add(square, note)
    self$play(Create(circle), run_time = 1.5, rate_func = linear)
    self$remove(note)
    self$play(square$animate$shift(RIGHT * 1.5), circle$animate$shift(LEFT * 1.5))
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

Named arguments of `self$play()` apply to every animation in the call:

* `run_time`: duration in seconds (most animations default to 1).
* `rate_func`: a function mapping the elapsed fraction of time, from 0 to
  1, to the fraction of the animation done. The default for most
  animations is `smooth_rate`, which starts and ends slowly. See
  [Rate functions](#rate-functions).
* `lag_ratio`: how much the submobjects of a group are staggered. With 0
  (the default for most animations) they all move together; with 1 each
  starts when the previous one ends; values in between overlap.

Several animations in one `self$play()` call start together, and the call
lasts as long as the longest of them. The next example plays the same
`FadeIn()` on two rows of squares, once with `lag_ratio = 0` and once with
`lag_ratio = 0.5`.

```{manim lag-ratio}
LagRatio <- R6::R6Class("LagRatio", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    together <- VGroup(lapply(1:6, function(i) Square(side_length = 0.8, color = BLUE, fill_opacity = 0.7)))
    together$arrange(RIGHT)$shift(UP * 1.2 + RIGHT)
    staggered <- together$copy()$set_color(ORANGE)$shift(DOWN * 2.4)
    labels <- VGroup(
      Text("lag_ratio = 0", font_size = 28)$next_to(together, LEFT, buff = 0.5),
      Text("lag_ratio = 0.5", font_size = 28)$next_to(staggered, LEFT, buff = 0.5)
    )
    self$add(labels)
    self$play(FadeIn(together, shift = UP), FadeIn(staggered, shift = UP, lag_ratio = 0.5), run_time = 2)
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

Waiting has three variants:

* `self$wait(duration)` holds the frame for `duration` seconds (1 by
  default) while updaters keep running.
* `self$pause(duration)` holds a frozen frame: updaters do not run, which
  renders faster.
* `self$wait_until(stop_condition, max_time)` waits until a function
  returns `TRUE`. It is covered in [Updaters and value
  trackers](updaters.html).

Under the hood every `self$wait()` plays a `Wait()` animation, so
`self$play(Wait(1))` is the same as `self$wait(1)`.

## The `$animate` builder

Every mobject has an `$animate` field. Calling methods on it records them
instead of applying them, and the result is an animation that morphs the
mobject from its current state to the state after those calls. Methods can
be chained, exactly as on the mobject itself.

Animation arguments such as `run_time` and `rate_func` can be given in two
places: to `self$play()`, or by calling `$animate` like a function before
the first method, as in `mob$animate(run_time = 2)$shift(RIGHT)`. This is
the R spelling of upstream manim's `mob.animate(run_time=2).shift(RIGHT)`.

```{manim animate-builder}
AnimateBuilder <- R6::R6Class("AnimateBuilder", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    square <- Square(color = BLUE, fill_opacity = 0.5)
    self$add(square)
    self$play(square$animate$shift(LEFT * 3)$scale(0.5)$set_color(YELLOW))
    self$play(square$animate(run_time = 2, rate_func = linear)$shift(RIGHT * 6))
    self$play(square$animate$rotate(PI / 4)$set_fill(RED, opacity = 0.8), run_time = 0.75)
  })
)
```

Two details to keep in mind:

* The builder morphs between two snapshots. It does not replay the method
  calls frame by frame, so `square$animate$rotate(PI)` looks like a flip
  through the center rather than a turn. Use `Rotate()` for a real
  rotation.
* Two builders on the same mobject in one `self$play()` call do not
  combine; the last one wins. Chain the methods in a single builder
  instead.

By default every point travels in a straight line. The `path_arc`
argument makes points travel along an arc of that angle instead; positive
angles bend counterclockwise.

```{manim animate-path-arc}
AnimatePathArc <- R6::R6Class("AnimatePathArc", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    straight_path_line <- Line(LEFT * 4 + UP, RIGHT * 4 + UP, color = GREY, stroke_width = 2)
    arc_path_line <- ArcBetweenPoints(LEFT * 4 + DOWN, RIGHT * 4 + DOWN, angle = PI / 2, color = GREY, stroke_width = 2)
    straight <- Dot(LEFT * 4 + UP, radius = 0.15, color = BLUE)
    arced <- Dot(LEFT * 4 + DOWN, radius = 0.15, color = ORANGE)
    self$add(straight_path_line, arc_path_line, straight, arced)
    self$play(straight$animate$shift(RIGHT * 8), arced$animate(path_arc = PI / 2)$shift(RIGHT * 8), run_time = 2)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`self$play()` accepts builders and animation objects alike: it converts
builders with `prepare_animation()`, which you can also call yourself, for
example to inspect or store an animation before playing it.

```{r prepare-animation}
builder <- Square()$animate$shift(RIGHT)$scale(2)
builder
anim <- prepare_animation(builder)
anim
anim$run_time
```

## Creation

These animations draw a mobject onto the screen, or remove it the way it
was drawn. The "create" style animations add the mobject to the scene when
they start, so there is no need to call `self$add()` first.

* `Create()` draws the outline of a VMobject along its path.
* `DrawBorderThenFill()` draws the outline, then fills it.
* `Write()` draws each submobject's border and fill in turn, the classic
  handwriting effect for text. Its run time and lag ratio default to values
  based on the number of submobjects; `reverse = TRUE` writes from the end.

```{manim creation-basics}
CreationBasics <- R6::R6Class("CreationBasics", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    circle <- Circle(color = BLUE)$shift(LEFT * 4)
    square <- Square(color = GREEN, fill_opacity = 0.6)
    word <- Text("Write", color = YELLOW)$shift(RIGHT * 4)
    self$play(Create(circle))
    self$play(DrawBorderThenFill(square), run_time = 1.5)
    self$play(Write(word))
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

`Uncreate()` and `Unwrite()` run `Create()` and `Write()` backwards and
remove the mobject from the scene when they finish.

```{manim uncreate-unwrite}
UncreateUnwrite <- R6::R6Class("UncreateUnwrite", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    circle <- Circle(color = BLUE)$shift(LEFT * 3)
    word <- Text("Unwrite", color = YELLOW)$shift(RIGHT * 3)
    note <- Text("Uncreate and Unwrite remove the mobject at the end", font_size = 28)$to_edge(DOWN)
    self$add(circle, word, note)
    self$wait(0.3)
    self$play(Uncreate(circle), Unwrite(word))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`SpiralIn()` flies the submobjects of a group in from far away while
spinning them into place. `scale_factor` sets how far out they start.

```{manim spiral-in}
SpiralInExample <- R6::R6Class("SpiralInExample", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    shapes <- VGroup(
      Circle(radius = 0.8, color = BLUE, fill_opacity = 0.5)$shift(LEFT * 2.5),
      Square(color = GREEN, fill_opacity = 0.5),
      Triangle(color = RED, fill_opacity = 0.5)$shift(RIGHT * 2.5)
    )
    self$play(SpiralIn(shapes, scale_factor = 3), run_time = 2)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`ShowIncreasingSubsets()` reveals the submobjects of a group one after
another and keeps them; `ShowSubmobjectsOneByOne()` shows only one at a
time, so the last one stays at the end.

```{manim subsets}
Subsets <- R6::R6Class("Subsets", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    top <- VGroup(lapply(1:8, function(i) Dot(radius = 0.2, color = BLUE)))$arrange(RIGHT, buff = 0.5)$shift(UP)
    bottom <- top$copy()$set_color(ORANGE)$shift(DOWN * 2)
    self$add(
      Text("ShowIncreasingSubsets", font_size = 28)$next_to(top, UP),
      Text("ShowSubmobjectsOneByOne", font_size = 28)$next_to(bottom, UP)
    )
    self$play(ShowIncreasingSubsets(top), ShowSubmobjectsOneByOne(bottom), run_time = 2)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

Text has its own creation animations. Each glyph of a `Text()` is a
submobject, so `AddTextLetterByLetter()` shows it one letter at a time
(`time_per_char` seconds per letter) and `RemoveTextLetterByLetter()`
removes it the same way. `AddTextWordByWord()` takes a group whose
submobjects are words, here a `VGroup` of `Text()` objects.

```{manim letter-by-letter}
LetterByLetter <- R6::R6Class("LetterByLetter", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    first <- Text("AddTextLetterByLetter", font_size = 40)$shift(UP * 1.5)
    second <- Text("RemoveTextLetterByLetter", font_size = 40)
    words <- VGroup(lapply(c("one", "word", "at", "a", "time"), Text, font_size = 40))
    words$arrange(RIGHT, aligned_edge = DOWN)$shift(DOWN * 1.5)
    self$play(AddTextLetterByLetter(first, time_per_char = 0.05))
    self$add(second)
    self$play(RemoveTextLetterByLetter(second, time_per_char = 0.05))
    self$play(AddTextWordByWord(words))
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

`TypeWithCursor()` types a text while a cursor mobject moves along it, and
`UntypeWithCursor()` deletes it again. `Blink()` (an indication animation)
makes the cursor blink in between.

```{manim typing}
Typing <- R6::R6Class("Typing", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    text <- Text("Typing", color = PURPLE)$scale(1.5)$to_edge(LEFT)
    cursor <- Rectangle(color = GREY_A, fill_color = GREY_A, fill_opacity = 1, height = 1.1, width = 0.5)
    cursor$move_to(text[1])
    self$play(TypeWithCursor(text, cursor))
    self$play(Blink(cursor, blinks = 2, time_on = 0.25, time_off = 0.25))
    self$play(UntypeWithCursor(text, cursor))
    done <- Text("Done", color = YELLOW)$scale(1.5)$to_edge(LEFT)
    self$play(TypeWithCursor(done, cursor))
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

`ShowPartial` is the base class of `Create()` and `ShowPassingFlash()`: at
each moment it shows the part of the path between two proportions returned
by its `get_bounds(alpha)` method. Subclass `ShowPartialClass` to define a
new way of revealing a path. This one grows the path from its middle
outward; the circle's middle is its leftmost point because circles start
at the right.

```{manim show-partial}
ShowFromMiddle <- R6::R6Class("ShowFromMiddle", inherit = ShowPartialClass,
  public = list(
    initialize = function(mobject, ...) super$initialize(mobject, introducer = TRUE, ...),
    get_bounds = function(alpha) c(0.5 - alpha / 2, 0.5 + alpha / 2)
  )
)
ShowPartialExample <- R6::R6Class("ShowPartialExample", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    line <- Line(LEFT * 5, RIGHT * 5, color = TEAL)$shift(UP * 2)
    circle <- Circle(radius = 1.5, color = YELLOW)$shift(DOWN * 0.8)
    self$play(ShowFromMiddle$new(line), ShowFromMiddle$new(circle), run_time = 2)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

## Fading

`FadeIn()` and `FadeOut()` change the opacity, optionally combined with a
movement or a scale change:

* `shift`: a vector to move along while fading (in from `-shift` for
  `FadeIn()`, out toward `shift` for `FadeOut()`).
* `target_position`: a point or mobject to fade from (`FadeIn()`) or to
  (`FadeOut()`).
* `scale`: the scale of the invisible state, so `FadeIn(m, scale = 0.2)`
  grows while appearing.

Both accept several mobjects at once, as in `FadeOut(a, b, c)`.

```{manim fading}
Fading <- R6::R6Class("Fading", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    square <- Square(color = BLUE, fill_opacity = 0.5)$shift(LEFT * 4)
    circle <- Circle(color = GREEN, fill_opacity = 0.5)
    triangle <- Triangle(color = YELLOW, fill_opacity = 0.5)$shift(RIGHT * 4)
    self$play(FadeIn(square, shift = DOWN), FadeIn(circle, scale = 0.2), FadeIn(triangle, target_position = ORIGIN))
    self$play(FadeOut(square, shift = DOWN), FadeOut(triangle, target_position = circle, scale = 0.5))
    self$play(FadeIn(Text("FadeIn and FadeOut", font_size = 36)$to_edge(UP), shift = DOWN))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

## Growing

Growing animations scale a mobject up from nothing:

* `GrowFromPoint(mobject, point)` from any point (or the center of a mobject).
* `GrowFromCenter(mobject)` from its own center.
* `GrowFromEdge(mobject, edge)` from one of its edges, such as `DOWN`.
* `GrowArrow(arrow)` from the start of an arrow, keeping the tip in shape.
* `SpinInFromNothing(mobject, angle)` grows while spinning by `angle`.

`point_color` sets the color the mobject starts with.

```{manim growing}
Growing <- R6::R6Class("Growing", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    shapes <- list(
      Square(side_length = 1.6, color = BLUE, fill_opacity = 0.5),
      Circle(radius = 0.8, color = GREEN, fill_opacity = 0.5),
      Rectangle(width = 1, height = 1.8, color = RED, fill_opacity = 0.5),
      Arrow(LEFT, RIGHT, color = YELLOW),
      Star(outer_radius = 0.9, color = PURPLE, fill_opacity = 0.5)
    )
    titles <- c("GrowFromPoint", "GrowFromCenter", "GrowFromEdge", "GrowArrow", "SpinInFromNothing")
    xs <- c(-5.4, -2.7, 0, 2.7, 5.4)
    for (i in seq_along(shapes)) {
      shapes[[i]]$move_to(RIGHT * xs[i] + UP * 0.5)
      self$add(Text(titles[i], font_size = 20)$move_to(RIGHT * xs[i] + DOWN * 1.2))
    }
    self$play(
      GrowFromPoint(shapes[[1]], ORIGIN),
      GrowFromCenter(shapes[[2]]),
      GrowFromEdge(shapes[[3]], DOWN),
      GrowArrow(shapes[[4]]),
      SpinInFromNothing(shapes[[5]], point_color = WHITE),
      run_time = 1.5
    )
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

## Indication

Indication animations draw attention to something without changing it for
good. They are listed in `?indication`.

* `Indicate()` briefly scales a mobject up and colors it (`scale_factor`,
  `color`).
* `Circumscribe()` runs a frame around it, a rectangle by default or a
  circle with `shape = "circle"`; `fade_in` and `fade_out` fade the frame
  instead of drawing it.
* `Wiggle()` shakes it (`scale_value`, `rotation_angle`, `n_wiggles`).
* `ApplyWave()` sends a wave through it (`direction`, `amplitude`,
  `ripples`).

```{manim indication-text}
IndicationText <- R6::R6Class("IndicationText", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    words <- VGroup(lapply(c("Indicate", "Circumscribe", "Wiggle", "ApplyWave"), Text, font_size = 40))
    words$arrange(DOWN, buff = 0.5)
    self$add(words)
    self$play(Indicate(words[1]))
    self$play(Circumscribe(words[2]))
    self$play(Circumscribe(words[2], shape = "circle", fade_out = TRUE, color = BLUE))
    self$play(Wiggle(words[3], run_time = 1))
    self$play(ApplyWave(words[4], run_time = 1))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

The second group works on points and paths:

* `Flash()` sends short lines out from a point (`num_lines`,
  `flash_radius`, `line_length`).
* `FocusOn()` shrinks a large translucent spotlight onto a point.
* `ShowPassingFlash()` shows only a short piece of a path (`time_width`, a
  fraction of the path) traveling along it, and removes it at the end.
* `ShowPassingFlashWithThinningStrokeWidth()` does the same with a tail
  that gets thinner.
* `Blink()` switches the opacity of a mobject off and on (`blinks`,
  `time_on`, `time_off`, `hide_at_end`).

```{manim indication-points}
IndicationPoints <- R6::R6Class("IndicationPoints", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    dot <- Dot(LEFT * 3, radius = 0.15, color = YELLOW)
    ring <- Circle(radius = 1.2, color = BLUE)$shift(RIGHT * 3)
    self$add(dot, ring)
    self$play(Flash(dot, flash_radius = 0.3, num_lines = 10))
    self$play(FocusOn(dot, run_time = 1))
    self$play(ShowPassingFlash(ring$copy()$set_color(YELLOW), time_width = 0.3))
    self$play(ShowPassingFlashWithThinningStrokeWidth(ring$copy()$set_stroke(YELLOW, width = 10), time_width = 0.4))
    self$play(Blink(dot, blinks = 2, time_on = 0.2, time_off = 0.2))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

## Movement

A homotopy is a function of a point and time. `Homotopy(homotopy, mobject)`
takes a function `function(x, y, z, t)` that returns the new point, and
applies it to every point of the mobject for `t` going from 0 to 1.
`SmoothedVectorizedHomotopy()` does the same but smooths the curves after
each step, so corners round off. A homotopy moves the existing points
only, so give shapes with few points more of them first with
`insert_n_curves()`.

```{manim homotopy}
HomotopyExample <- R6::R6Class("HomotopyExample", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    wave <- function(x, y, z, t) c(x, y + 0.35 * t * sin(3 * x), z)
    word <- Text("Homotopy", font_size = 72)$shift(UP * 1.5)
    plain <- Square(side_length = 2, color = BLUE)$insert_n_curves(12)$shift(LEFT * 3 + DOWN * 1.5)
    smoothed <- plain$copy()$set_color(ORANGE)$shift(RIGHT * 6)
    self$add(word, plain, smoothed)
    self$play(Homotopy(wave, word), Homotopy(wave, plain), SmoothedVectorizedHomotopy(wave, smoothed), run_time = 2)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`ComplexHomotopy()` is the same with a function `function(z, t)` of a
complex number `z = x + iy`. `PhaseFlow()` moves every point along a vector
field `function(p)` for `virtual_time` units of time. Both work in scene
coordinates, so the homotopy below squares each point relative to the
center of the square rather than relative to the origin. The flow on the
right is a shear: points move sideways in proportion to their height.

```{manim complex-homotopy}
FlowExample <- R6::R6Class("FlowExample", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    center <- -3.5 + 0i
    square <- Square(side_length = 2.4, color = BLUE)$insert_n_curves(16)$move_to(c(Re(center), Im(center), 0))
    # Squares each point relative to the center of the square, blended in as t grows.
    squaring <- function(z, t) {
      w <- z - center
      center + (1 - t) * w + t * w^2 / 2
    }
    grid <- VGroup(lapply(1:16, function(i) Square(side_length = 0.6, color = YELLOW)))
    grid$arrange_in_grid(4, 4, buff = 0)$shift(RIGHT * 3)
    shear <- function(p) c(0.6 * p[2], 0, 0)
    self$add(square, grid)
    self$play(ComplexHomotopy(squaring, square), PhaseFlow(shear, grid, virtual_time = 1), run_time = 2)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`MoveAlongPath(mobject, path)` moves a mobject so that its center follows
a path.

```{manim move-along-path}
MoveAlongPathExample <- R6::R6Class("MoveAlongPathExample", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    path <- FunctionGraph(function(x) 1.5 * sin(x), x_range = c(-5, 5), color = GREY)
    dot <- Dot(path$point_from_proportion(0), radius = 0.15, color = YELLOW)
    self$add(path, dot)
    self$play(MoveAlongPath(dot, path), run_time = 2, rate_func = linear)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

## Rotation

`Rotate(mobject, angle)` turns a mobject by `angle` radians around its
center, or around `about_point`; points travel along circles, so even a
full turn (`angle = TAU`) is visible. `Rotating()` spins a mobject
continuously at a constant speed (`rate_func = linear` by default) and
is handy for many turns; its default run time is 5 seconds.

```{manim rotation}
RotationExample <- R6::R6Class("RotationExample", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    square <- Square(color = BLUE, fill_opacity = 0.5)$shift(LEFT * 4)
    bar <- Rectangle(width = 2, height = 0.3, color = GREEN, fill_opacity = 0.8)
    sun <- Dot(RIGHT * 4, radius = 0.3, color = YELLOW)
    planet <- Dot(RIGHT * 4 + UP * 1.5, radius = 0.15, color = TEAL)
    self$add(square, bar, sun, planet)
    self$play(
      Rotate(square, angle = PI / 4),
      Rotate(bar, angle = PI / 2, about_point = bar$get_left()),
      Rotating(planet, angle = PI, about_point = RIGHT * 4, run_time = 2)
    )
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

## Transforms

`Transform(a, b)` morphs `a` into the shape and style of `b`. Two related
animations differ in what is on screen afterwards:

* After `Transform(a, b)`, the mobject on screen is still `a` (it now
  looks like `b`); `b` itself was never added. Keep working with `a`.
* After `ReplacementTransform(a, b)`, `a` is gone and `b` is on screen.
  Keep working with `b`.

```{manim transform-vs-replacement}
TransformVsReplacement <- R6::R6Class("TransformVsReplacement", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    left_square <- Square(color = BLUE)$shift(LEFT * 3)
    left_circle <- Circle(color = BLUE)$shift(LEFT * 3)
    right_square <- Square(color = ORANGE)$shift(RIGHT * 3)
    right_circle <- Circle(color = ORANGE)$shift(RIGHT * 3)
    self$add(
      Text("Transform", font_size = 28)$move_to(LEFT * 3 + DOWN * 2),
      Text("ReplacementTransform", font_size = 28)$move_to(RIGHT * 3 + DOWN * 2),
      left_square, right_square
    )
    self$play(Transform(left_square, left_circle), ReplacementTransform(right_square, right_circle))
    # Animate the mobject that is on screen now.
    self$play(left_square$animate$set_fill(BLUE, opacity = 0.6), right_circle$animate$set_fill(ORANGE, opacity = 0.6))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`TransformFromCopy(a, b)` leaves `a` in place and morphs a copy of it into
`b`. `ClockwiseTransform()` and `CounterclockwiseTransform()` are
`Transform()` with points moving along half circles (`path_arc = -pi` and
`path_arc = pi`).

```{manim transform-copy-arcs}
TransformCopyArcs <- R6::R6Class("TransformCopyArcs", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    source <- Square(side_length = 1, color = BLUE, fill_opacity = 0.5)$shift(LEFT * 4 + UP * 2.5)
    target <- Circle(radius = 0.6, color = GREEN, fill_opacity = 0.5)$shift(RIGHT * 4 + UP * 2.5)
    self$add(source)
    self$play(TransformFromCopy(source, target))
    a <- Triangle(color = RED)$scale(0.5)$shift(LEFT * 2 + DOWN * 2)
    b <- Square(side_length = 0.8, color = RED)$shift(RIGHT * 2 + DOWN * 2)
    self$add(a)
    self$play(ClockwiseTransform(a, b))
    c_shape <- Star(outer_radius = 0.5, color = YELLOW)$shift(RIGHT * 2 + UP * 0.5)
    d_shape <- Circle(radius = 0.4, color = YELLOW)$shift(LEFT * 2 + UP * 0.5)
    self$add(c_shape)
    self$play(CounterclockwiseTransform(c_shape, d_shape))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

### Targets, methods and saved states

`MoveToTarget()` works with `generate_target()`: the method stores a copy
of the mobject in `mob$target`, you change that copy freely, and
`MoveToTarget(mob)` morphs the mobject into it. `ApplyMethod()` takes a
method of a mobject (written without calling it, as `circle$shift`) and its
arguments, which is what `circle$animate$shift(...)` does for you.
`save_state()` stores a copy of a mobject and `Restore()` morphs back to it.

`FadeToColor()`, `ScaleInPlace()` and `ShrinkToCenter()` are shortcuts for
recoloring, scaling about the center, and scaling to nothing.

```{manim targets-and-methods}
TargetsAndMethods <- R6::R6Class("TargetsAndMethods", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    circle <- Circle(color = BLUE)$shift(LEFT * 4)
    circle$save_state()
    circle$generate_target()
    circle$target$shift(RIGHT * 2)$scale(0.5)$set_color(YELLOW)
    square <- Square(color = GREEN)$shift(RIGHT * 1.5)
    triangle <- Triangle(color = PURPLE)$shift(RIGHT * 4.5)
    self$add(circle, square, triangle)
    self$play(MoveToTarget(circle))
    self$play(ApplyMethod(circle$shift, UP * 1.5))
    self$play(Restore(circle))
    self$play(FadeToColor(square, RED), ShrinkToCenter(triangle))
    self$play(ScaleInPlace(square, 0.5))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

### Applying functions

These animations compute the target by applying a function:

* `ApplyFunction(fn, mob)`: `fn` receives a copy of the mobject and
  returns the modified mobject.
* `ApplyPointwiseFunction(fn, mob)`: `fn` maps each point (a numeric
  vector `c(x, y, z)`) to a new point.
* `ApplyPointwiseFunctionToCenter(fn, mob)`: moves the whole mobject so
  that its center goes to `fn(center)`.
* `ApplyMatrix(matrix, mob)`: applies a 2 x 2 or 3 x 3 matrix to every
  point, about `about_point` (the origin by default).

`ApplyPointwiseFunction()` and `ApplyMatrix()` default to a run time of 3
seconds.

```{manim apply-functions}
ApplyFunctions <- R6::R6Class("ApplyFunctions", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    places <- list(LEFT * 3.5 + UP * 1.6, RIGHT * 3.5 + UP * 1.6, LEFT * 3.5 + DOWN * 2, RIGHT * 3.5 + DOWN * 2)
    titles <- c("ApplyFunction", "ApplyPointwiseFunction", "ApplyPointwiseFunctionToCenter", "ApplyMatrix")
    shapes <- lapply(1:4, function(i) Square(side_length = 1.5, color = BLUE)$insert_n_curves(8)$move_to(places[[i]]))
    for (i in 1:4) self$add(shapes[[i]], Text(titles[i], font_size = 24)$next_to(shapes[[i]], UP))
    self$play(ApplyFunction(function(m) m$scale(0.6)$rotate(PI / 4)$set_color(YELLOW), shapes[[1]]))
    self$play(ApplyPointwiseFunction(function(p) p + c(0, 0.25 * sin(3 * p[1]), 0), shapes[[2]], run_time = 1.5))
    self$play(ApplyPointwiseFunctionToCenter(function(p) p + RIGHT * 1.5, shapes[[3]]))
    shear <- matrix(c(1, 0, 1, 1), nrow = 2)
    self$play(ApplyMatrix(shear, shapes[[4]], about_point = shapes[[4]]$get_center(), run_time = 1.5))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`ApplyComplexFunction(fn, mob)` treats each point as the complex number
`x + iy` and moves it to `fn(x + iy)`. Shapes need extra points to bend
smoothly; a `NumberPlane` gets them from `prepare_for_nonlinear_transform()`.

```{manim apply-complex}
ApplyComplex <- R6::R6Class("ApplyComplex", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    plane <- NumberPlane(x_range = c(-1, 1, 0.25), y_range = c(-1.5, 1.5, 0.25))
    plane$prepare_for_nonlinear_transform()
    self$add(plane)
    self$play(ApplyComplexFunction(exp, plane), run_time = 2)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

### Swapping places and cross fading

`CyclicReplace(a, b, c)` moves each mobject to the position of the next
one, and the last to the first; `Swap(a, b)` is the same for two. Both move
along arcs (`path_arc = 90 * DEGREES` by default).

`FadeTransform(a, b)` cross fades instead of morphing points: `a` fades
out while stretching to the shape of `b`, and `b` fades in from the shape
of `a`. `FadeTransformPieces()` does this submobject by submobject.

```{manim swap-and-fade}
SwapAndFade <- R6::R6Class("SwapAndFade", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    shapes <- VGroup(Square(color = BLUE), Circle(color = GREEN), Triangle(color = RED))
    shapes$arrange(RIGHT, buff = 1)$scale(0.6)$shift(UP * 2)
    self$add(shapes)
    self$play(CyclicReplace(shapes[1], shapes[2], shapes[3]))
    self$play(Swap(shapes[1], shapes[3]))
    one <- VGroup(Square(color = TEAL), Circle(color = TEAL))$arrange(RIGHT)$scale(0.6)$shift(LEFT * 3 + DOWN * 1.5)
    two <- VGroup(Triangle(color = ORANGE), Star(color = ORANGE))$arrange(RIGHT)$scale(0.6)$shift(LEFT * 3 + DOWN * 1.5)
    three <- one$copy()$shift(RIGHT * 6)
    four <- two$copy()$shift(RIGHT * 6)
    self$add(one, three)
    self$play(FadeTransform(one, two), FadeTransformPieces(three, four), run_time = 1.5)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

## Transforming matching parts

`TransformMatchingShapes(a, b)` pairs up submobjects of the same shape and
moves each one to its partner; parts without a partner fade out or in.
With `Text()` this makes anagrams, because each letter is a submobject.

```{manim matching-shapes}
MatchingShapes <- R6::R6Class("MatchingShapes", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    source <- Text("the morse code", font_size = 60)
    target <- Text("here come dots", font_size = 60)
    self$play(Write(source))
    self$play(TransformMatchingShapes(source, target, path_arc = PI / 2), run_time = 1.5)
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

`TransformMatchingTex(a, b)` does the same for `MathTex()` objects, matching
the parts by their LaTeX strings. Split the formula into parts by passing
several strings, or with double braces, as `"{{a}}^2"` below. Parts that
should move into a part with a different string can be paired with
`key_map`, for example `key_map = c("+" = "-")`. This chunk needs LaTeX.

```{manim matching-tex, eval = has_latex}
MatchingTex <- R6::R6Class("MatchingTex", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    eq1 <- MathTex("{{a}}^2", "+", "{{b}}^2", "=", "{{c}}^2", font_size = 72)
    eq2 <- MathTex("{{a}}^2", "=", "{{c}}^2", "-", "{{b}}^2", font_size = 72)
    self$add(eq1)
    self$wait(0.3)
    self$play(TransformMatchingTex(eq1, eq2, key_map = c("+" = "-")), run_time = 1.5)
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

Both accept `transform_mismatches = TRUE` (morph unmatched parts into each
other with `Transform()`) and `fade_transform_mismatches = TRUE` (use
`FadeTransformPieces()` for them).

## Composing animations

Four helpers combine animations into one:

* `AnimationGroup(...)` plays animations together; with `lag_ratio`, each
  one starts after that fraction of the previous one's run time.
* `Succession(...)` plays them one after another (it is an
  `AnimationGroup()` with `lag_ratio = 1`).
* `LaggedStart(...)` is an `AnimationGroup()` with a small default
  `lag_ratio` of 0.05.
* `LaggedStartMap(animation_class, group, ...)` applies an animation
  constructor to every submobject of a group, passing the remaining named
  arguments on, and staggers the results.

All of them take animations or lists of animations, so `lapply()` output
can be passed directly. The composed animation can be nested in another,
and `run_time` or `rate_func` on it apply to the whole schedule.

```{manim composition}
Composition <- R6::R6Class("Composition", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    rows <- lapply(1:4, function(i) {
      VGroup(lapply(1:6, function(j) Square(side_length = 0.6, color = BLUE, fill_opacity = 0.6)))$arrange(RIGHT, buff = 0.2)
    })
    VGroup(rows)$arrange(DOWN, buff = 0.5)$shift(RIGHT * 2)
    titles <- c("AnimationGroup", "Succession", "LaggedStart", "LaggedStartMap")
    for (i in 1:4) self$add(Text(titles[i], font_size = 28)$next_to(rows[[i]], LEFT, buff = 0.6))
    self$play(AnimationGroup(lapply(rows[[1]]$submobjects, GrowFromCenter), lag_ratio = 0.3))
    self$play(Succession(lapply(rows[[2]]$submobjects, function(m) FadeIn(m, run_time = 0.2))))
    self$play(LaggedStart(lapply(rows[[3]]$submobjects, function(m) FadeIn(m, shift = DOWN)), lag_ratio = 0.25))
    self$play(LaggedStartMap(FadeIn, rows[[4]], shift = UP, lag_ratio = 0.25, run_time = 1))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`Wait()` and `Add()` are useful inside `Succession()`: `Wait(t)` does
nothing for `t` seconds and `Add(mob)` puts mobjects on screen instantly at
that point of the schedule. `Broadcast(mob)` sends expanding copies of a
mobject out from `focal_point` (`n_mobs` copies, 3 seconds by default) and
removes them at the end.

```{manim wait-add-broadcast}
WaitAddBroadcast <- R6::R6Class("WaitAddBroadcast", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    circle <- Circle(color = BLUE)$shift(LEFT * 4)
    square <- Square(color = GREEN)$shift(RIGHT * 4)
    self$play(Succession(Add(circle), Wait(0.5), Create(square)))
    self$play(Broadcast(Circle(radius = 2, color = YELLOW), n_mobs = 4, run_time = 2))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

## Animating numbers

`ChangeDecimalToValue(decimal, value)` counts a `DecimalNumber()` to a new
value, and `ChangingDecimal(decimal, fn)` sets it to `fn(alpha)` as the
animation progresses from `alpha = 0` to `alpha = 1`. `DecimalNumber()`
typesets digits with `MathTex()` by default; `mob_class = Text` uses
system fonts instead, so this example does not need LaTeX.

```{manim number-animations}
NumberAnimations <- R6::R6Class("NumberAnimations", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    counter <- DecimalNumber(0, num_decimal_places = 1, mob_class = Text, font_size = 96)
    self$add(counter)
    self$play(ChangeDecimalToValue(counter, 100), run_time = 2)
    self$play(ChangingDecimal(counter, function(alpha) 100 - 50 * alpha^2), run_time = 1.5)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

Number labels that follow a moving value are usually built with updaters
instead; see [Updaters and value trackers](updaters.html).

## Changing the speed

`ChangeSpeed(anim, speedinfo)` plays an animation (or a builder) at a
varying speed. `speedinfo` is a named vector: the names are points of the
animation, as fractions from 0 to 1, and the values are speed factors
there. Between two points the speed changes smoothly, and the run time
stretches or shrinks to match.

Updaters normally ignore such speed changes. An updater added with
`change_speed_add_updater()` instead of `mob$add_updater()` follows the
speed of a playing `ChangeSpeed()` animation, so the orange dot below slows
down together with the blue one.

```{manim change-speed}
ChangeSpeedExample <- R6::R6Class("ChangeSpeedExample", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    a <- Dot(LEFT * 5 + UP, radius = 0.15, color = BLUE)
    b <- Dot(LEFT * 5 + DOWN, radius = 0.15, color = ORANGE)
    self$add(a, b)
    # The updater stops the dot at x = 5, where the blue dot ends.
    change_speed_add_updater(b, function(m, dt) m$set_x(min(m$get_x() + 10 * dt, 5)))
    self$play(ChangeSpeed(
      a$animate$shift(RIGHT * 10),
      speedinfo = c("0.3" = 1, "0.4" = 0.1, "0.6" = 0.1, "1" = 1),
      rate_func = linear
    ))
    b$clear_updaters()
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`ChangeSpeedClass$add_updater()` is the same function under the name used
by upstream manim.

## Rate functions

A rate function maps time `t` in `[0, 1]` to progress, also mostly in
`[0, 1]`. manimR has all of upstream manim's rate functions (see
`?rate_funcs`); upstream's `smooth` is called `smooth_rate` in R so that it
does not mask `stats::smooth()`. The [Utilities](utilities.html) vignette
shows a gallery of all of them. These are plain R functions of a single
number:

```{r rate-function-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 101)
funs <- list(linear = linear, smooth_rate = smooth_rate, rush_into = rush_into,
             there_and_back = there_and_back, ease_out_bounce = ease_out_bounce)
values <- sapply(funs, function(f) vapply(t, f, numeric(1)))
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
matplot(t, values, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, xlab = "t", ylab = "rate_func(t)")
legend("topleft", names(funs), col = 1:5, lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(op)
```

Any function of `t` works as a rate function, and two helpers build new
ones from old: `squish_rate_func(f, a, b)` runs `f` between times `a` and
`b` only, and `not_quite_there(f, proportion)` stops short.

```{manim rate-functions}
RateFunctions <- R6::R6Class("RateFunctions", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    funs <- list(
      linear = linear,
      smooth_rate = smooth_rate,
      rush_from = rush_from,
      there_and_back = there_and_back,
      ease_out_bounce = ease_out_bounce,
      "squish_rate_func(smooth_rate, 0.4, 1)" = squish_rate_func(smooth_rate, 0.4, 1),
      "function(t) t^3" = function(t) t^3
    )
    ys <- seq(3, -3, length.out = length(funs))
    dots <- lapply(seq_along(funs), function(i) Dot(c(-0.5, ys[i], 0), color = YELLOW))
    for (i in seq_along(funs)) {
      self$add(Text(names(funs)[i], font_size = 22)$next_to(c(-0.8, ys[i], 0), LEFT), dots[[i]])
    }
    self$play(lapply(seq_along(funs), function(i) dots[[i]]$animate(rate_func = funs[[i]])$shift(RIGHT * 6)), run_time = 2)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

## Path functions

While a transform runs, a path function decides the route each point
takes from its start to its end. Pass one as `path_func` to `Transform()`
and its relatives (and to `$animate`), or use the `path_arc` shortcut
shown earlier, which builds `path_along_arc(path_arc)` for you. The
available path functions (see `?paths`) are:

* `straight_path()`: the default.
* `path_along_arc(arc_angle, axis)`: along an arc of `arc_angle` radians.
* `clockwise_path()` and `counterclockwise_path()`: half circles.
* `spiral_path(angle)`: the travel direction turns by `angle` on the way,
  so the shape also rotates.
* `path_along_circles(arc_angle, circles_centers)`: around fixed centers,
  as `Rotate()` uses.

```{manim path-functions}
PathFunctions <- R6::R6Class("PathFunctions", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    labels <- c("straight_path()", "path_along_arc(PI / 2)", "spiral_path(-PI / 2)")
    ys <- c(2.5, 0, -2.5)
    starts <- lapply(ys, function(y) Square(side_length = 0.8, color = BLUE)$move_to(c(-3, y, 0)))
    ends <- lapply(ys, function(y) Square(side_length = 0.8, color = ORANGE)$rotate(PI / 4)$move_to(c(3, y, 0)))
    for (i in 1:3) self$add(starts[[i]], Text(labels[i], font_size = 22)$next_to(c(-4, ys[i], 0), LEFT))
    self$play(Transform(starts[[1]], ends[[1]], path_func = straight_path()))
    self$play(Transform(starts[[2]], ends[[2]], path_func = path_along_arc(PI / 2)))
    self$play(Transform(starts[[3]], ends[[3]], path_func = spiral_path(-PI / 2)))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

A path function is an R function `function(start_points, end_points,
alpha)` that returns the interpolated points (n x 3 matrices), so you can
call one directly, or write your own. Here is where a point traveling from
`(-1, 0)` to `(1, 0)` is halfway along each path:

```{r path-midpoints}
start <- matrix(c(-1, 0, 0), nrow = 1)
end <- matrix(c(1, 0, 0), nrow = 1)
path_list <- list(
  straight = straight_path(),
  arc = path_along_arc(PI / 2),
  clockwise = clockwise_path(),
  counterclockwise = counterclockwise_path(),
  spiral = spiral_path(PI / 2),
  circles = path_along_circles(PI / 2, ORIGIN)
)
halfway <- t(sapply(path_list, function(f) f(start, end, 0.5)))
colnames(halfway) <- c("x", "y", "z")
round(halfway, 3)
```

## Changing defaults

`set_default()` changes the default arguments of a mobject or animation
class for every later call, and `set_default(cls)` with no other arguments
restores the original defaults. The scene below makes every `FadeIn()`
rise from below and every `Create()` last two seconds, and resets both when
`construct()` exits.

```{manim set-default}
SetDefaultExample <- R6::R6Class("SetDefaultExample", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    set_default(FadeIn, shift = UP)
    set_default(Create, run_time = 2)
    on.exit({
      set_default(FadeIn)
      set_default(Create)
    })
    self$play(FadeIn(Square(color = BLUE)$shift(LEFT * 3)))
    self$play(Create(Circle(color = GREEN)$shift(RIGHT * 3)))
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`MobjectClass$set_default()` and `AnimationClass$set_default()` are the
same for the two base classes, as in upstream manim.

## Overriding animations for a class

A mobject class can decide how a standard animation looks for its objects.
`override_animation(class, "FadeIn", fn)` makes `FadeIn(obj)` call
`fn(...)` as a method of `obj` (so `self` is available) and play whatever
it returns. This is the R form of upstream's `@override_animation`
decorator. Pass `use_override = FALSE` to get the normal animation.

```{manim override-animation}
Tile <- R6::R6Class("Tile", inherit = SquareClass, lock_objects = FALSE)
override_animation(Tile, "FadeIn", function(...) SpinInFromNothing(self, angle = PI, ...))
OverrideAnimationExample <- R6::R6Class("OverrideAnimationExample", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    tile <- Tile$new(color = YELLOW, fill_opacity = 0.6)$shift(LEFT * 2.5)
    plain <- Tile$new(color = BLUE, fill_opacity = 0.6)$shift(RIGHT * 2.5)
    self$play(FadeIn(tile), FadeIn(plain, use_override = FALSE), run_time = 1.5)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

`override_animate(class, "method", fn)` customizes `obj$animate$method()`,
like upstream's `@override_animate`. The function receives the method's
arguments plus `anim_args`, the arguments given to `$animate(...)`, and
returns an animation. Here clearing the content of a circle uncreates the
content, instead of the default morph.

```{manim override-animate}
CircleWithContent <- R6::R6Class("CircleWithContent", inherit = VGroupClass, lock_objects = FALSE,
  public = list(
    circle = NULL,
    content = NULL,
    initialize = function(content) {
      super$initialize()
      self$circle <- Circle(color = BLUE)
      self$content <- content
      self$add(self$circle, content)
      content$move_to(self$circle$get_center())
    },
    clear_content = function() {
      self$remove(self$content)
      self$content <- NULL
      invisible(self)
    }
  )
)
override_animate(CircleWithContent, "clear_content", function(anim_args = list()) {
  anim <- do.call(Uncreate, c(list(self$content), anim_args))
  self$clear_content()
  anim
})
OverrideAnimateExample <- R6::R6Class("OverrideAnimateExample", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    holder <- CircleWithContent$new(Square(side_length = 1, color = YELLOW))
    self$add(holder)
    self$wait(0.3)
    self$play(holder$animate(run_time = 1.5)$clear_content())
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

Both functions change the class in place, so they apply to every object
created afterwards, including objects of subclasses. Use them on your own
classes; overriding a built in class changes it for the rest of the R
session.

## Writing your own animation

An animation is an R6 class that inherits from `AnimationClass` (the
generator behind `Animation()`). The playing scene calls three methods:

* `begin()` once at the start. The default stores a copy of the mobject in
  `self$starting_mobject` and calls `interpolate(0)`.
* `interpolate_mobject(alpha)` on every frame, with `alpha` going from 0
  to 1 in linear time. Apply `self$rate_func(alpha)` yourself when you
  override this method; the default implementation does it for you and
  calls `interpolate_submobject()` on each submobject with a staggered
  alpha (this is where `lag_ratio` comes in).
* `finish()` once at the end. The default calls `interpolate(1)`.

The animation below grows a mobject from nothing while it spins and fades
from white to its own color. `begin()` remembers that color before the
first frame, and `finish()` gives the result a thicker outline.
`introducer = TRUE` adds the mobject to the scene when the animation
starts, as `Create()` does.

```{manim custom-animation}
SpinIn <- R6::R6Class("SpinIn", inherit = AnimationClass,
  public = list(
    angle = TAU,
    color = NULL,
    initialize = function(mobject, angle = TAU, ...) {
      self$angle <- angle
      super$initialize(mobject, introducer = TRUE, ...)
    },
    begin = function() {
      self$color <- self$mobject$get_color()
      super$begin()
    },
    interpolate_mobject = function(alpha) {
      a <- self$rate_func(alpha)
      self$mobject$become(self$starting_mobject)
      self$mobject$scale(max(a, 0.001))
      self$mobject$rotate(a * self$angle)
      self$mobject$set_color(interpolate_color(WHITE, self$color, a))
    },
    finish = function() {
      super$finish()
      self$mobject$set_stroke(width = 8)
    }
  )
)
CustomAnimation <- R6::R6Class("CustomAnimation", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    square <- Square(color = BLUE, fill_opacity = 0.5)$shift(LEFT * 2.5)
    star <- Star(color = YELLOW, fill_opacity = 0.5)$shift(RIGHT * 2.5)
    self$play(SpinIn$new(square), SpinIn$new(star, angle = -PI), run_time = 1.5)
    self$wait(0.3)
  })
)
```

Create the animation with `SpinIn$new(...)`, or wrap it in a function such
as `spin_in <- function(mobject, ...) SpinIn$new(mobject, ...)` to get the
same calling style as the built in constructors. Arguments that you do not
handle yourself (`run_time`, `rate_func`, `lag_ratio` and so on) pass
through `...` to `AnimationClass`, and arguments of `self$play()` reach
your animation as usual.
